M6.Synapse.Title: Modeling connections: the synapse
M6.Synapse.Lead: Neurons talk through synapses. A presynaptic spike releases neurotransmitter, which opens ion channels in the postsynaptic membrane and briefly changes its conductance. The computational model keeps exactly this chain: a time-varying conductance g_s(t) with a reversal potential E_s, added as an extra branch to the RC membrane.
M6.Synapse.C1.Title: Excitation or inhibition is decided by E_s
M6.Synapse.C1.Text: The synaptic current I_s = g_s(V − E_s) always pushes V towards E_s. If E_s lies above the threshold (AMPA, ≈ 0 mV) the synapse depolarizes – it is excitatory. If E_s lies below rest (GABA_A, ≈ −80 mV) it hyperpolarizes – inhibitory. If E_s sits close to rest (shunting inhibition) the membrane hardly moves, yet the extra open conductance short-circuits every other input.
M6.Synapse.C2.Title: Channel kinetics: P_s opens and closes
M6.Synapse.C2.Text: P_s is the fraction of open postsynaptic channels (or, for one channel, its open probability). α_s is the opening, β_s the closing rate. A spike drives P_s up quickly, after which it decays with the closing rate. The conductance is g_s = g_s,max · P_rel · P_s, where P_rel is the probability that transmitter is released.
M6.Synapse.C3.Title: The synapse is a temporal filter
M6.Synapse.C3.Text: The effect of one spike lasts for milliseconds: the channels open, then close on a characteristic time scale. Some synapses are well described by an exponential kernel (instant rise, exp(−t/τ_s)), others by an alpha function (smooth rise, peak at τ). With many spikes the conductance is the sum of the filtered effects of earlier spikes – the synapse both weights and smears the spike train in time. NMDA responses are much slower than AMPA responses.
M6.Synapse.C4.Title: Two neurons: the sign changes the rhythm
M6.Synapse.C4.Text: Coupling just two integrate-and-fire neurons already gives qualitatively different collective dynamics. In the lecture's example excitatory coupling produces alternating firing, inhibitory coupling synchrony. The timing of a network is shaped not only by its neuron model but by the sign, strength and time constant of its connections.
M6.Synapse.Formulas:
I_s(t) = g_s(t) · (V − E_s) | Synaptic current: it always drives V towards the reversal potential E_s.
τ_m dV/dt = −(V − E_L) − r_m g_s(t)(V − E_s) + R_m I_e | Membrane with a synaptic branch: leak + synapse + injected current.
dP_s/dt = α_s (1 − P_s) − β_s P_s | Opening (α_s) and closing (β_s) of the postsynaptic channels; g_s = g_s,max · P_rel · P_s.
K(t) = exp(−t/τ_s)     α(t) = (t/τ) · exp(1 − t/τ) | Single-spike time courses: exponential and alpha kernel.
M6.Synapse.Bio: Glutamate acting on AMPA receptors opens cation channels (E ≈ 0 mV) within a millisecond, which close again within a few ms. NMDA receptors are much slower (tens to hundreds of ms) and also voltage-dependent (Mg²⁺ block). GABA_A receptors open chloride channels (E ≈ −70 … −80 mV). Electrical synapses (gap junctions) exist too, but most communication between neurons is chemical.
M6.Synapse.Takeaways:
A synapse is modeled as a time-varying conductance with its own reversal potential.
Whether it excites or inhibits is decided by where E_s lies relative to V and the threshold – not simply by a sign.
A spike's effect is filtered in time (exponential or alpha kernel); AMPA is fast, NMDA slow.
Many spikes add up: the conductance is the sum of the filtered effects of past spikes.
The sign and time constants of connections shape network rhythms: in the example, excitation → alternation, inhibition → synchrony.
M6.Synapse.Q1: Why can a synapse be described as a time-varying conductance?
M6.Synapse.A1: Because after a spike, postsynaptic ion channels open with a characteristic time course; their momentary current is g_s(t)(V − E_s).
M6.Synapse.Q2: What is the role of the reversal potential in excitatory and inhibitory synapses?
M6.Synapse.A2: It decides in which direction the synaptic current drives the membrane potential: above threshold it depolarizes (excitatory), below rest it hyperpolarizes (inhibitory).
M6.Synapse.Q3: What does the variable P_s mean in the postsynaptic channel model?
M6.Synapse.A3: The fraction of open postsynaptic channels, or the open probability of one channel.
M6.Synapse.Q4: Why can the synapse be regarded as a temporal filter?
M6.Synapse.A4: Because after an instantaneous spike the conductance does not vanish at once but decays according to a kernel – the input spike train is smoothed in time.
M6.Synapse.Q5: How do two coupled integrate-and-fire neurons behave with excitatory and with inhibitory synapses?
M6.Synapse.A5: In the lecture's example excitatory coupling gives alternating (anti-phase) firing, inhibitory coupling gives synchronous firing.
M6.Synapse.Guide:
Press “GABA_A”: E_s jumps to −80 mV and every input spike pushes V down.
Press “AMPA”: now spikes depolarize and the cell fires more.
Try “Shunting”: E_s is close to rest, V barely moves – yet firing drops.
Switch on the alpha kernel and raise τ_s: the conductance becomes smooth and slow (NMDA-like).
Below, switch the pair between excitatory and inhibitory and watch the rhythm change.
M6.Synapse.SimpleTitle: In plain words: a door that lets charge in or out
M6.Synapse.Simple: A synapse is like a small door in the wall of the receiving cell. When a signal (spike) arrives, the door opens for a moment and then slowly closes. What flows through depends on what waits behind the door: at an “encouraging” (excitatory) synapse positive charge flows in and pushes the cell towards firing; at a “calming” (inhibitory) one the flow pulls it away from firing. The dashed E_s line shows where the door is trying to pull the voltage. Click the synapse types and watch the curve: with GABA every arriving spike makes a small dip, with AMPA a small bump.
M6.Synapse.Types.Tip: Typical parameter sets of real synapses: transmitter, reversal potential and time constant.
M6.Synapse.Preset.AMPA: Fast glutamatergic synapse: E_s = 0 mV, τ_s = 3 ms → excitatory.
M6.Synapse.Preset.GABA: GABA_A synapse: chloride channels, E_s = −80 mV, τ_s = 8 ms → inhibitory (hyperpolarizing).
M6.Synapse.Preset.NMDA: Slow glutamatergic synapse: alpha kernel with τ = 40 ms – long-lasting, strongly summing input.
M6.Synapse.Preset.Shunting: Shunting inhibition: E_s = −68 mV, close to rest. Little visible hyperpolarization, but the open conductance cancels other input.
M6.Synapse.Es.Tip: The voltage at which the synaptic current reverses. The synapse pulls V towards E_s: above threshold it excites, below rest it inhibits.
M6.Synapse.Strength.Tip: Peak synaptic conductance relative to the leak conductance (dimensionless).
M6.Synapse.Tau.Tip: Decay time of the exponential kernel, or peak time of the alpha kernel.
M6.Synapse.Alpha.Tip: Off: exponential kernel exp(−t/τ) with an instant rise. On: α(t) = (t/τ)·exp(1 − t/τ), peaking at t = τ.
M6.Synapse.Rate.Tip: Firing rate of the presynaptic neuron.
M6.Synapse.Background.Tip: Constant depolarizing current that keeps the cell close to threshold (16 mV above rest is needed to fire).
M6.Synapse.Poisson.Tip: On: irregular spike times as in vivo. Off: a perfectly regular spike train.
M6.Synapse.Inject.Tip: Delivers one presynaptic spike now – watch a single postsynaptic potential.
M6.Synapse.Scope.Tip: Top: membrane potential V(t) with threshold, rest and E_s. Bottom: synaptic conductance r_m·g_s(t) – every jump is one presynaptic spike.
M6.Synapse.Readout: V = {0} mV   r_m·g_s = {1}   synaptic drive = {2} mV   output ≈ {3} Hz
M6.Synapse.Explain.Exc: E_s = {0} mV lies {1} mV above the threshold: every open channel pulls V upwards – the synapse is excitatory.
M6.Synapse.Explain.Inh: E_s = {0} mV lies below the resting potential: the synaptic current pulls V downwards – the synapse is inhibitory (hyperpolarizing).
M6.Synapse.Explain.Shunt: E_s = {0} mV is close to rest: V hardly moves, but the open conductance short-circuits the background drive – shunting inhibition reduces firing without a visible dip.
M6.Synapse.Pair.Tip: Two integrate-and-fire neurons drive each other through alpha synapses (Dayan & Abbott, fig. 5.20). Top trace: neuron A, bottom trace: neuron B.
M6.Synapse.Pair.Readout: Phase of B within A's cycle: {0} (0 = synchronous, 0.5 = anti-phase) → {1}
M6.Feedforward.Title: Network models: feedforward filtering
M6.Feedforward.Lead: The first decision in network modeling: do we follow every spike, or only firing rates? Rate models lose precise timing but make large networks analyzable. In a firing-rate feedforward network the inputs form a vector u, the outputs a vector v, the connections a weight matrix W – and the network becomes a linear filter.
M6.Feedforward.C1.Title: Spiking or firing-rate models?
M6.Feedforward.C1.Text: Spiking networks keep spike timing, correlations and synchrony, but they are expensive to simulate. Firing-rate models replace many spikes by one real-valued rate per neuron: cheaper and much easier to analyze, but blind to precise spike timing.
M6.Feedforward.C2.Title: Many inputs, one weighted sum
M6.Feedforward.C2.Text: A neuron with N inputs sums the filtered spike trains, each weighted by its synaptic weight w_b. In the rate approximation this becomes a dot product w·u; with many outputs a matrix product W u. Every row of W is one output neuron's pattern of input weights – its receptive field.
M6.Feedforward.C3.Title: A linear network is a filter
M6.Feedforward.C3.Text: If F is linear, the steady state is simply v = W u. When every row of W contains the same, shifted kernel, W performs a convolution. The lecture's kernel [0, −1, 1, 0, 0] is a discrete derivative: large positive or negative response where the input changes quickly, near zero on smooth, constant regions – edge detection.
M6.Feedforward.C4.Title: From 1-D edges to V1
M6.Feedforward.C4.Text: The same idea in two dimensions highlights changes of brightness and contrast in an image. Receptive fields in the primary visual cortex (V1) are selective for edges, orientations and local contrast – linear filtering is the first model of what they compute.
M6.Feedforward.Formulas:
I_s(t) = Σ_b w_b ∫ K(t − τ) ρ_b(τ) dτ | Total synaptic current: weighted sum of the filtered input spike trains ρ_b.
τ dv/dt = −v + F(W u) | Firing-rate dynamics of a feedforward layer with activation function F.
v_ss = W u | Linear steady state: the output is a matrix–vector product.
row i of W = [0, −1, 1, 0, 0] shifted to i | Discrete derivative kernel: v_i = u_i − u_(i−1).
M6.Feedforward.Bio: Retinal ganglion cells and LGN neurons have centre–surround receptive fields; V1 simple cells respond best to oriented edges and bars. Their responses are well approximated by linear filtering of the image followed by a nonlinearity – the Vision page of the lab shows the 2-D version.
M6.Feedforward.ML: A layer v = F(W u) is exactly a fully connected layer of an artificial neural network. A Toeplitz W (one kernel shared by all positions) is a 1-D convolution – the building block of convolutional networks.
M6.Feedforward.Takeaways:
Firing-rate models trade spike timing for simplicity and scale.
Many inputs → weighted sum; many outputs → weight matrix W; each row is one neuron's receptive field.
A linear feedforward network settles to v = W u.
Shared, shifted kernels turn W into a convolution; the derivative kernel detects edges.
M6.Feedforward.Q1: What is the main trade-off between spiking and firing-rate network models?
M6.Feedforward.A1: Spiking models keep timing and synchrony but are costly; rate models are efficient and analyzable but lose precise spike timing.
M6.Feedforward.Q2: How does the weighted sum of many inputs become the matrix operation W·u?
M6.Feedforward.A2: Put the input rates into a vector u and each output neuron's weights into a row of W; every output is the dot product of its row with u.
M6.Feedforward.Q3: Why is a linear feedforward network an edge-detecting filter?
M6.Feedforward.A3: With a suitable weight pattern it computes local intensity differences – a discrete derivative – which is large at edges and near zero on flat regions.
M6.Feedforward.Q4: What does the row of W of an output neuron describe biologically?
M6.Feedforward.A4: Its receptive field: which inputs excite it, which inhibit it and how strongly.
M6.Feedforward.Guide:
Hover over an output neuron in the network diagram: its incoming weights light up (red +, blue −).
With the derivative kernel choose the “Bar” input: the output peaks at both edges, with opposite signs.
Switch to centre–surround: both edges give a double response.
Try the noisy bar with the smoothing kernel – the noise is averaged away.
Press “Restart relaxation” and watch v approach W u with time constant τ.
M6.Feedforward.SimpleTitle: In plain words: a row of detectors that compare neighbours
M6.Feedforward.Simple: Imagine a row of people, each looking at two neighbouring lamps of a light strip. Everyone shouts only if their right lamp is brighter than their left one. Where the strip is evenly lit, everybody stays quiet; where dark turns into bright, someone shouts loudly. That is edge detection – and it is nothing but a “weighted sum” of what each person sees. The table that says who looks at which lamp with what weight is the matrix W.
M6.Feedforward.Input.Tip: Firing rates of the 48 input neurons.
M6.Feedforward.Kernel.Tip: Every output neuron uses the same local weight pattern, shifted to its own position.
M6.Feedforward.Explain.Derivative: Discrete derivative: v_i = u_i − u_(i−1). Constant regions give 0, a rising edge a positive and a falling edge a negative response – edge detection.
M6.Feedforward.Explain.CenterSurround: Centre minus the mean of its neighbours: zero on flat and linear regions, strong on both sides of an edge and on thin bars – like retinal ganglion cells.
M6.Feedforward.Explain.Smoothing: Local averaging: sharp edges are blurred and random noise is reduced – a low-pass filter.
M6.Feedforward.Explain.Identity: W = I: every output copies its own input; the network only adds the time constant τ.
M6.Feedforward.Restart.Tip: Sets v = 0 and lets the network relax to W u following τ dv/dt = −v + W u.
M6.Feedforward.Matrix.Tip: Rows: output neurons i, columns: inputs j. Pink = negative, teal = positive weight. Hover a row to select that output neuron.
M6.Feedforward.Network.Tip: Top row: input neurons (brightness = rate). Bottom row: output neurons (teal positive, pink negative). Hover to select a neuron and see its incoming connections.
M6.Feedforward.Profiles.Tip: Bars: input rates u. Teal line: current output v(t); dotted line: steady state W u.
M6.Linear.Title: Recurrent networks I: eigenmodes, amplification, memory
M6.Linear.Lead: In a recurrent network the output is fed back as input: τ dv/dt = −v + h + M v. The network acquires its own dynamics – the same momentary input can give different outputs depending on what happened before. For a symmetric M the eigenvectors turn the coupled system into independent modes.
M6.Linear.C1.Title: Three competing terms
M6.Linear.C1.Text: −v makes activity decay, h drives it from outside, M v feeds the network's own activity back. Their competition decides whether the activity dies out, is amplified, persists, oscillates or becomes unstable.
M6.Linear.C2.Title: Eigenvectors are activity patterns
M6.Linear.C2.Text: A symmetric M has N orthonormal eigenvectors e_i (M e_i = λ_i e_i) that form a basis: any activity pattern is a combination v = Σ c_i e_i. In neuroscience terms e_i is a characteristic pattern of the whole population (a mode), and its eigenvalue λ_i tells how strongly recurrent feedback reinforces or weakens it.
M6.Linear.C3.Title: Every mode is a leaky integrator
M6.Linear.C3.Text: Projected onto e_i, the N coupled equations fall apart into independent scalar ones: τ dc_i/dt = −(1 − λ_i)c_i + h·e_i. Mode i relaxes with the effective time constant τ/(1 − λ_i) to c_i = (h·e_i)/(1 − λ_i). With λ = 0.9 the input component along e_i is amplified tenfold – selectively, not every signal.
M6.Linear.C4.Title: λ = 1: integration and memory
M6.Linear.C4.Text: For λ = 1 the decay term vanishes: τ dc/dt = h·e. The mode integrates its input and, when the input stops, keeps the value it reached – persistent activity. The memory is in the dynamical state of the network, not in a separate store. λ > 1 is unstable: activity grows without bound.
M6.Linear.Formulas:
τ dv/dt = −v + h + M v | Linear recurrent network: decay, external drive, feedback.
M e_i = λ_i e_i,    v(t) = Σ_i c_i(t) e_i | Eigen-decomposition: activity as a sum of modes.
τ dc_i/dt = −(1 − λ_i) c_i + h·e_i | Each mode evolves on its own.
c_i,ss = (h·e_i) / (1 − λ_i) | Steady state: gain 1/(1 − λ_i) – e.g. ×10 for λ = 0.9.
M(θ, θ′) ∝ cos(θ − θ′) | Ring connectivity: similar preferences excite, opposite ones inhibit.
M6.Linear.Bio: Neurons of the brainstem oculomotor integrator turn brief velocity bursts into sustained firing proportional to eye position – a near-perfect integrator with λ ≈ 1. Mistuning makes the eye drift back to the centre (λ < 1) or away from it (λ > 1), as observed in some patients.
M6.Linear.ML: Discrete-time RNNs face the same question: the eigenvalues of the recurrent weight matrix decide whether information fades (|λ| < 1), is kept (|λ| ≈ 1) or explodes (|λ| > 1) – the root of the vanishing / exploding gradient problem.
M6.Linear.Takeaways:
The M v term feeds the network's own activity back: the system gets an internal state and dynamics.
For symmetric M, eigenvectors are population activity modes and eigenvalues set their dynamics.
λ < 1: stable decay; λ near 1: strong, slow amplification; λ = 1: integration and memory; λ > 1: runaway.
Amplification is selective: only the input component along the eigenvector is boosted.
M6.Linear.Q1: What does the M v term mean in the recurrent equation?
M6.Linear.A1: The recurrent feedback: the network's current output, weighted by the connection matrix, acts as additional input.
M6.Linear.Q2: What does an eigenvector represent in the activity space of a population?
M6.Linear.A2: A characteristic activity pattern (mode) of the whole population that the feedback only scales, never turns into another pattern.
M6.Linear.Q3: What happens to a mode when λ approaches 1? And when λ = 1?
M6.Linear.A3: Its gain 1/(1 − λ) grows and its decay slows down; at λ = 1 it integrates the input and keeps the value after the input is gone.
M6.Linear.Q4: What is the steady-state amplification for λ = 0.9?
M6.Linear.A4: 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10: the input component along that eigenvector is amplified tenfold.
M6.Linear.Guide:
Pick “Amplifier (0.9)”, then press the right pulse: c jumps and slowly leaks back.
Pick “Integrator (1.0)”: each pulse moves c to a new level that stays – the eye holds its gaze.
Use left pulses to bring the eye back.
Try λ = 1.03: activity runs away even without input.
In the ring below raise λ towards 1: the noisy input turns into a large, smooth cosine bump.
M6.Linear.SimpleTitle: In plain words: an echo that fades, rings on or lasts forever
M6.Linear.Simple: Imagine shouting in a hall. In a hall with soft walls (small λ) the echo fades at once. With hard walls (λ close to 1) the echo lasts long and makes your voice louder. In a perfect hall (λ = 1) the sound never fades – the hall “remembers” your shout. If the walls even amplified the sound (λ > 1), the echo would grow louder and louder. The eye on the left uses exactly this: a short “look right” command is remembered, so the eye stays where it was sent.
M6.Linear.Eigenvalue.Tip: λ of the eigenmode: how strongly the recurrent feedback reinforces this activity pattern.
M6.Linear.Lambda.Tip: λ < 1 stable, λ = 1 perfect integrator, λ > 1 unstable.
M6.Linear.Sustained.Tip: Constant input projected onto the mode. With λ < 1 the mode settles at h·e/(1 − λ); with λ = 1 it ramps up linearly.
M6.Linear.Pulse.Tip: A 50 ms burst of input – like a saccade command to the eye muscles.
M6.Linear.Eye.Tip: The gaze direction follows the stored value c of the mode.
M6.Linear.Eye.Text: Gaze = c(t). With λ = 1 the eye stays where the last burst sent it; with λ < 1 it drifts back to the centre.
M6.Linear.Mode.Tip: Teal: the amplitude c(t) of the mode. Yellow: the input h·e (drawn ×10).
M6.Linear.Explain.None: λ = 0: no feedback – the mode simply follows its input with time constant τ.
M6.Linear.Explain.Negative: λ < 0: negative feedback – the mode is suppressed and reacts faster than τ.
M6.Linear.Explain.Stable: λ = {0}: stable. The input is amplified by 1/(1 − λ), and after the input stops the activity decays with τ_eff = {1} ms.
M6.Linear.Explain.Integrator: λ ≈ 1: the decay term vanishes – the mode integrates its input and holds the value: persistent activity, a memory.
M6.Linear.Explain.Unstable: λ > 1: feedback is stronger than the leak – any small activity grows exponentially. Real networks need a nonlinearity to stop this (next lesson).
M6.Linear.Ring.Tip: 72 neurons with preferred directions and cosine connectivity M_ij ∝ cos(θ_i − θ_j). The cosine modes have eigenvalue λ, all others 0.
M6.Linear.Ring.Readout: input peak {0} → output peak {1}    (cosine-mode gain 1/(1 − λ) = {2})
M6.Linear.Ring.Unstable: λ ≥ 1 – the linear ring is unstable, the output grows without limit (clipped on the plot).
M6.Nonlinear.Title: Recurrent networks II: nonlinear dynamics
M6.Nonlinear.Lead: Firing rates cannot be negative, and real neurons saturate. With a nonlinearity, τ dv/dt = −v + F(h + M v), a recurrent network can use strong feedback without exploding – and gains collective functions: cleaning noisy input, choosing between competitors, scaling responses and holding a memory.
M6.Nonlinear.C1.Title: Rectification keeps rates positive
M6.Nonlinear.C1.Text: F(x) = [x]⁺ cuts negative drive to zero. Only part of the ring is active at a time, so the effective feedback within the active group is limited: strong recurrent excitation no longer leads to infinite activity. A saturating F also caps the maximal rate.
M6.Nonlinear.C2.Title: Selective amplification and winner-takes-all
M6.Nonlinear.C2.Text: Similarly tuned neurons excite each other, competing populations inhibit each other. A weak, structured bump hidden in noise is amplified into a clean activity profile. If two input peaks compete, the network makes one dominant and suppresses the other – a model of selective attention.
M6.Nonlinear.C3.Title: Gain modulation
M6.Nonlinear.C3.Text: Adding an almost constant background to the input of a nonlinear recurrent network does not simply shift the output: the tuning curve keeps its shape while its amplitude is scaled. An additive change of the input becomes an almost multiplicative change of the output.
M6.Nonlinear.C4.Title: Persistent activity and working memory
M6.Nonlinear.C4.Text: With strong enough recurrence a brief local input leaves behind a self-sustaining population bump at the cued location, even after the input has gone. Here the memory is not a lasting synaptic change but an active state of the network – a simple computational model of working memory that holds information for seconds.
M6.Nonlinear.Formulas:
τ dv/dt = −v + F(h + M v) | Nonlinear recurrent network.
F(x) = [x]⁺ = x if x > 0, else 0 | Rectification: negative drive gives zero rate.
M_ij = (−J₀ + 2J₁ cos(θ_i − θ_j)) / N | Ring: J₁ local excitation (λ of the cosine modes), J₀ global inhibition.
h(θ) + b  →  approx. g(b) · v(θ) | Gain modulation: an additive background scales the output.
M6.Nonlinear.Bio: Prefrontal neurons keep firing during the delay period of memory tasks (persistent activity); head-direction cells form a ring attractor whose activity bump follows the animal's heading; attention scales tuning curves in visual cortex multiplicatively (gain modulation).
M6.Nonlinear.ML: Winner-takes-all and attractor dynamics reappear in Hopfield networks, in softmax competition and in attention mechanisms; the bump attractor is the continuous counterpart of a stored memory pattern.
M6.Nonlinear.Takeaways:
A nonlinearity (rectification, saturation) keeps strong feedback bounded.
Local excitation + broad inhibition → selective amplification and winner-takes-all.
Gain modulation: additive input changes become multiplicative output changes.
Persistent activity is memory stored in the network state, not in the synaptic weights.
M6.Nonlinear.Q1: Why is the nonlinearity essential in recurrent networks?
M6.Nonlinear.A1: Without it strong feedback (effective eigenvalue > 1) makes the activity grow without bound; rectification and saturation limit the growth, so new stable states can appear.
M6.Nonlinear.Q2: How can winner-takes-all selection arise in a nonlinear recurrent network?
M6.Nonlinear.A2: Through local positive feedback and competing, inhibitory connections: one input pattern is reinforced, the other suppressed.
M6.Nonlinear.Q3: What is persistent activity and why can it model working memory?
M6.Nonlinear.A3: Activity that remains after the input is gone; the earlier state is kept by the network's dynamics for seconds, without any weight change.
M6.Nonlinear.A4: Scaling the amplitude of a response while the shape of the tuning stays roughly the same – here produced by an additive background input.
M6.Nonlinear.Guide:
“Selective amplification”: a weak bump buried in noise becomes a clean, much larger profile.
“Winner-takes-all”: two cues compete and only the stronger survives – change the amplitude to swap the winner.
“Gain modulation”: the dashed curves share the same shape at different heights. Change the background and freeze the curve.
“Working memory”: the cue flashes for 250 ms – the bump remains. Move the cue and flash again.
M6.Nonlinear.SimpleTitle: In plain words: a crowd that agrees, competes and remembers
M6.Nonlinear.Simple: Picture people standing in a circle, each responsible for one direction. Neighbours encourage each other, people far apart hush each other. If someone quietly points “north” in a noisy crowd, the northern neighbours join in and soon a clear “NORTH!” rises above the noise. If two groups point different ways, the louder group wins and silences the other. And if the encouragement is strong enough, the group keeps shouting “north” even after the original pointer has fallen silent – the crowd remembers.
M6.Nonlinear.Scenarios.Tip: Each preset sets up the ring for one phenomenon of lecture 6.3.
M6.Nonlinear.Explain.Amplify: A weak bump (amplitude 4) hidden in strong noise: rectification and local excitation (J₁ = 1.9) turn it into a clean bump several times higher – the noise outside is silenced.
M6.Nonlinear.Explain.Wta: Two cues 180° apart, one slightly stronger. Global inhibition (J₀) makes them compete: the network keeps one bump and suppresses the other.
M6.Nonlinear.Explain.Gain: The dashed curves are steady states for backgrounds b = 0, 3 and 6: the same tuning shape with different amplitudes – an additive input acts multiplicatively.
M6.Nonlinear.Explain.Memory: The cue is shown for only 250 ms. Strong recurrence (J₁ = 3) with saturating neurons keeps the bump alive afterwards – persistent activity at the cued direction.
M6.Nonlinear.Network.Tip: Activation function and connection strengths of the ring.
M6.Nonlinear.J1.Tip: Strength of the cosine-shaped connections between similarly tuned neurons – the eigenvalue of the cosine modes.
M6.Nonlinear.J0.Tip: Uniform inhibition between all neurons; it drives the competition.
M6.Nonlinear.Background.Tip: Constant input to every neuron (gain modulation).
M6.Nonlinear.InputOn.Tip: Switch the external input off to test whether the activity persists.
M6.Nonlinear.Flash.Tip: Shows the cue for 250 ms, then removes it.
M6.Nonlinear.RingView.Tip: Every neuron sits at its preferred direction. Outer bars: firing rate; inner dots: external input; arrow: population vector (decoded direction).
M6.Nonlinear.Peak.Tip: Maximum firing rate in the network – shows whether the activity settles, persists or dies out.
M6.Nonlinear.Profile.Tip: Yellow: input h(θ). Teal: network output v(θ). Dashed: frozen curves for comparison.
M6.Nonlinear.Freeze.Tip: Keeps the current output profile on the plot for comparison (e.g. at different backgrounds).
M6.Nonlinear.Readout: max {0} Hz   active {1}/{2}   decoded direction {3}   input {4}
M6.Oscillation.Title: Recurrent networks III: excitation–inhibition oscillations
M6.Oscillation.Lead: When excitatory and inhibitory populations interact, the connection matrix is no longer symmetric and its eigenvalues can be complex. The real part decides whether perturbations grow or decay, the imaginary part makes the activity rotate – it oscillates.
M6.Oscillation.C1.Title: Two populations, one plane
M6.Oscillation.C1.Text: With one excitatory (v_E) and one inhibitory (v_I) population the state is a point in a plane. Excitation recruits inhibition, inhibition suppresses excitation, which in turn releases the inhibition – a natural loop that can become a rhythm.
M6.Oscillation.C2.Title: Stability from the Jacobian
M6.Oscillation.C2.Text: Linearize around the fixed point, where both derivatives are zero. The eigenvalues of the local stability matrix (Jacobian), λ = a ± bi, describe the behaviour nearby: a < 0 means decay, a > 0 growth; b ≠ 0 means rotation with frequency b/2π.
M6.Oscillation.C3.Title: Damped oscillation vs limit cycle
M6.Oscillation.C3.Text: With negative real part the activity spirals back into the fixed point – a damped oscillation. Changing a parameter (here the inhibitory time constant τ_I) can push the real part through zero: the fixed point loses stability, and the nonlinearity confines the growing spiral to a closed orbit – a limit cycle, a stable, sustained oscillation.
M6.Oscillation.C4.Title: Link to machine-learning recurrent networks
M6.Oscillation.C4.Text: Biological firing-rate networks and ML recurrent networks are different models, but share the core idea: the current state feeds back into the later state, providing temporal context and memory. The mathematical questions are the same: stability, strength of feedback, keeping information, and control of the state dynamics.
M6.Oscillation.Formulas:
τ_E dv_E/dt = −v_E + [M_EE v_E + M_EI v_I − γ_E]⁺ | Excitatory population.
τ_I dv_I/dt = −v_I + [M_IE v_E + M_II v_I − γ_I]⁺ | Inhibitory population.
J = [ (M_EE − 1)/τ_E   M_EI/τ_E ;  M_IE/τ_I   (M_II − 1)/τ_I ] | Jacobian at the fixed point.
λ = a ± bi:  a < 0 damped,  a > 0 growing,  f = b / 2π | Real part: stability; imaginary part: oscillation frequency.
M6.Oscillation.Bio: Loops between pyramidal cells and fast-spiking interneurons are thought to generate gamma (30–80 Hz) rhythms, whose period is set largely by the time course of inhibition. Pathologically strong excitation–inhibition loops can produce seizure-like oscillations (see the Network page of the lab).
M6.Oscillation.ML: In discrete-time RNNs and in linear dynamical systems, complex eigenvalues of the state-transition matrix also produce rotations; their modulus decides whether the rotation decays or grows. Several modern sequence models deliberately parametrize these eigenvalues to control memory and oscillation.
M6.Oscillation.Takeaways:
Non-symmetric (E–I) connectivity can have complex eigenvalues.
Real part → growth or decay; imaginary part → oscillation.
Damped oscillation: spiral into a stable fixed point; limit cycle: a stable closed orbit after the fixed point has lost stability.
The nonlinearity bounds the growth and creates the limit cycle.
M6.Oscillation.Q1: What do the real and imaginary parts of a complex eigenvalue indicate?
M6.Oscillation.A1: The real part growth (positive) or damping (negative); the imaginary part oscillation and its frequency.
M6.Oscillation.Q2: What is the difference between a damped oscillation and a limit cycle?
M6.Oscillation.A2: In a damped oscillation the amplitude decays towards a stable fixed point; on a limit cycle the periodic oscillation is sustained.
M6.Oscillation.Q3: Why are the eigenvalues of E–I networks often complex?
M6.Oscillation.A3: Because the connection matrix is not symmetric: excitation drives inhibition, inhibition suppresses excitation – a rotational interaction.
M6.Oscillation.A4: A network state at which the derivative of the state is zero, so it does not change.
M6.Oscillation.Guide:
“Damped (τ_I = 30 ms)”: the trajectory spirals into the fixed point.
Drag τ_I slowly past 40 ms and watch the eigenvalues cross the red Re = 0 line.
“Limit cycle (τ_I = 50 ms)”: the activity settles onto a closed orbit.
Click anywhere in the phase plane: from every start the system ends on the same cycle.
Compare the predicted frequency (imaginary part) with the period of the time traces.
M6.Oscillation.SimpleTitle: In plain words: an accelerator and a brake chasing each other
M6.Oscillation.Simple: The excitatory cells are the accelerator, the inhibitory cells the brake – and pressing the accelerator also presses the brake. When activity rises the brake engages; the brake slows everything down, so it is released again; then the accelerator wins again… If the brake reacts quickly, the swings die out (damped oscillation). If it reacts too slowly, the swings never stop and settle into a steady rhythm (limit cycle) – like a driver who keeps over-correcting.
M6.Oscillation.Params.Tip: Dayan & Abbott §7.5: M_EE = 1.25, M_EI = −1, M_IE = 1, M_II = 0, γ_E = −10 Hz, γ_I = 10 Hz, τ_E = 10 ms.
M6.Oscillation.TauI.Tip: Time constant of the inhibitory population. Slow inhibition destabilizes the fixed point: Hopf bifurcation at τ_I = 40 ms (for M_EE = 1.25).
M6.Oscillation.Mee.Tip: Strength of recurrent excitation. Stronger self-excitation also pushes the system towards oscillation.
M6.Oscillation.Kick.Tip: Pushes the state randomly away from the fixed point.
M6.Oscillation.Verdict.Damped: Stable spiral: the real part is negative, so perturbations decay while rotating at ≈ {0} Hz. (Critical τ_I = {1} ms.)
M6.Oscillation.Verdict.Cycle: Unstable spiral: the real part is positive. The nonlinearity stops the growth – a limit cycle at ≈ {0} Hz. (Critical τ_I = {1} ms.)
M6.Oscillation.Verdict.Node: Stable node: real eigenvalues, the activity returns without oscillating.
M6.Oscillation.Verdict.Saddle: Unstable fixed point with real eigenvalues: the activity escapes without rotating.
M6.Oscillation.Spectrum.Tip: Dots: the two eigenvalues of the Jacobian (1/s). Grey: their path as τ_I goes from 10 to 80 ms. Crossing the red line Re = 0 means losing stability.
M6.Oscillation.Phase.Tip: Arrows: direction of the flow. Green: v_E nullcline, violet: v_I nullcline – they cross at the fixed point. Yellow: trajectory. Click to start from a new state.
